title: Yudhishthira at Bhishma's bed of arrows
hookLine: a newly crowned king goes back to school, at the side of a dying elder
carry: vinaya: even a king stays a student
tomorrow: someone waits at the palace gate. how long is too long?
last: A JUST ROD IS A MEASURED ROD.

lines: AN ELDER ON A BED OF ARROWS.
cards: The war at Kurukshetra is over. Yudhishthira has won, and he's been crowned in Hastinapura. And he is still grieving.

So Krishna takes him back to the battlefield, to Bhishma, his great-uncle, lying on a bed of arrows and waiting for his time to die. Yudhishthira hangs back, ashamed: he led the army that brought this elder down.
But Bhishma welcomes him, and day after day the new king sits at the old man's side and asks: how should a king rule?

teach.b: Bhishma's answers fill whole books of the Mahabharata, its teaching on raja dharma. And the picture is a Hindu teaching in itself: the crown doesn't end the lessons.
The Arthashastra, this week's handbook, has a word for it: vinaya, discipline in the sense of being well taught.
It's frank: discipline is partly nature and partly learned, and teaching only shapes someone willing to be shaped. Where does a willing ruler find it?
With elders, it says, because discipline is rooted in them. So it fills the royal day: mornings on horses, elephants, chariots and weapons, afternoons hearing itihasa, the old accounts.
It's the same instinct that teaches Hindu children to touch an elder's feet and ask a blessing before anything big.
Now hold the week up. A bow to rival teachers, the way Kacha served Shukra. Gargi's questions, and reasoning as the lamp.

teach.h: THE CROWN IS WHERE LESSONS BEGIN.
teach.b: Victory over the senses, where Ravana failed. Manu's little fish, and power that protects the small. Mandavya's spike, and a rod in measure.
And under all of it, a king who never stops being a student.

how: Many Hindu families teach children to touch an elder's feet and ask a blessing before anything big, and to listen to the old stories; the Arthashastra's first book sets a prince's education with elders and itihasa, and the Mahabharata's Shanti Parva is Bhishma's teaching to a newly crowned king.

games.q: you've just been made lead on your shift at work. the person who trained you is still on the team. by vinaya, what now?
o: keep asking her advice, and actually listen to it.
stop asking. you're the lead now, and it looks weak.
move her to another shift so nobody second-guesses you.
games.why: in the Arthashastra, discipline is rooted in the elders, and a willing ruler keeps them close. Yudhishthira, newly crowned, sat at Bhishma's side to learn.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and bring to mind one elder whose words have stayed with you: a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor. If you pray, bow to them in your heart, the way many Hindu families touch an elder's feet.
Then let one thing they said come back, word for word if you can, and breathe with it, simply listening again.

wordCard.voice: The Arthashastra's opening: vinaya, a ruler's training, kept alive by the company of elders and the old stories.

orig.note: Sanskrit vinaya, training or discipline: the Arthashastra's word for a ruler's education.

carryVoice: Carry this: vinaya, even a king stays a student. Yudhishthira learned it at Bhishma's side. A week, done.
